# Notes Before the Campaign Meeting

*Written before the creative brief goes out, and before anyone has drawn a mood board. Campaigns assembled after the creative territories exist are not campaigns. They're a rationale for artwork somebody has already fallen in love with.*

---

## What we're actually selling

The brief says a campaign for a recently launched supplement. The brief is slightly wrong, or rather it's leading with the part that has a budget line attached.

A message is the most copyable thing in this category. Any competitor can run the same claim, the same shade of blue, the same lab-coat-adjacent visual language, within a season, and if they're less scrupulous than us they can run a *stronger* version of our claim, because the strongest claim is always available to whoever cares least. If our advantage is what we say, we've entered a race that is won by the least honest participant and lost slowly by everyone else.

What is not copyable in a season: a substantiation file that survives an unannounced regulatory demand, a relationship with the people behind a pharmacy counter, a purchase moment nobody else has noticed, a commercial model that doesn't depend on customers failing to cancel, and a reputation for saying less than we're legally allowed to.

So I'd treat the advertising as necessary and visible — it's what the market is equipped to see and what our own organisation is equipped to measure — and quietly spend the real effort on evidence, occasion, channel, and the cancellation flow. That ordering is the substance of these notes.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

"A specific market with unique social values" is a phrase carrying a great deal of luggage. I'm going to write as though we mean **Japan**, because it's the case where the reasoning is most testable, and because being wrong in a specific direction is more useful than being carefully vague. If someone in the room knows we mean Germany, or the Gulf, or Korea, this is the cheap moment to say so. Most of the structure transfers. Perhaps a third of the specifics don't.

Worth stating why it's the interesting case. An older population with an unusually high baseline supplement habit. A legal regime — the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act — under which a food may not imply it treats, prevents or diagnoses anything, and where the implication counts, not just the sentence. A separate law on representations under which the regulator can demand your substantiation and expect it in about a fortnight, with a surcharge on the relevant sales if you can't produce it. A tiered claims system where the light-touch notification route has just been through a very public crisis of confidence: the 2024 red-yeast-rice episode, kidney injuries, deaths reported, a national recall, and a subsequent tightening of the rules that everyone in the category is still absorbing.

And a cultural grammar in which overstatement reads as weakness. This is a market where the loudest advertiser in a health category is not the market leader — they're the one under investigation.

There's one more thing that makes it unusually workable, and I'll come back to it: almost every employed adult receives, once a year, an envelope containing numbers about their own body.

---

## What the research can and can't tell us

"Strong consumer interest in health and wellness" will be in the deck. It's true, it's true everywhere, and it describes what people say. Stated health intent is the single most inflated variable in consumer research, because agreeing that health matters costs nothing and admitting indifference costs a small amount of self-image.

The more useful question — which I'd put to research as a suggestion rather than a correction, because they'll get there faster if it's theirs — is not *what do people want to improve*. It's: **at what specific moment does a Japanese adult go from thinking about health to spending money on it?** And I'd propose the answer is rarely a moment of aspiration. It's a moment of mild, private, non-catastrophic bad news.

The annual health check result. The line on the printout that's in bold because it's outside the reference range, but not far outside, and not accompanied by a referral. Not illness. Not health. The market already has a word for it — **未病**, *mibyō*, the state before disease — which is a gift, because it means we don't have to teach the concept. It's several hundred years old and it's in the language.

That moment is currently served badly. It's served by a doctor with eleven minutes who says "watch your diet," by a spouse, by a search engine, and by a category of advertising that responds to a slightly elevated number with imagery of hospital beds. The inadequacy is the opportunity. Aspiration sells a first bottle. An inadequately served moment of quiet self-concern sells a habit measured in years.

---

## Ideas, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd float these rather than propose any. Which ones people reach for unprompted tells me more about the room than the ideas tell me about the market.

**1. The envelope — a bet on the occasion.**
Build the campaign's calendar around health-check result season rather than around New Year resolutions, which is where every competitor's media money sits. The creative territory is the twenty minutes after the envelope opens: a private, slightly deflating, entirely undramatic moment that advertising has never depicted because it isn't visually exciting. No fear imagery. No hospital. No before-and-after body. The tone is somebody reading a page at a kitchen table.

The ethical requirement that makes it work rather than compromises it: every execution carries the instruction to take the result to a physician. Not in eight-point type. In the line. A supplement brand that says *see your doctor first* is doing something no competitor will copy, because it costs conversion, and it buys the only thing worth buying here.

**2. The counter, not the shelf — a bet on the gatekeeper.**
Registered sellers and pharmacists in the drugstore chains are a real advisory layer, and the category treats them as a distribution surface. I'd treat them as the medium. Give them the actual evidence file — including the trial arms that didn't reach significance, the effect size in plain numbers, the interaction list, and a clear statement of who should not take this: people on specific medications, pregnancy and nursing, anyone under treatment for the relevant condition.

The bet is that the person who says *not this one, not for you* to one customer in five sells more over three years than the person who says yes to everyone. It's also structurally hard to replicate — a trained relationship across a few thousand counters isn't a media buy, it's two years of unglamorous field work.

**3. The undersell — a bet that restraint is now the differentiator.**
Print the ceiling. State the actual number from the actual trial — the duration, the sample size, the mean change — and state, in the advertisement itself, that some participants saw no change at all. Nobody does this. In a market recovering from a supplement scandal, an advertisement that visibly declines to oversell reads as confidence, and confidence is the scarce signal.

It is also, boringly, unassailable. Every sentence maps to a line in the dossier. When the regulator asks, the answer takes an afternoon, not a fortnight of panic.

I'd expect real resistance to this internally, which is one of the reasons I'd put it in the room early.

**4. The factory, not the body — a bet on traceability as narrative.**
After 2024, the live anxiety in this market is not *does it work*. It's *what is actually in it, and who checked*. So: lot-level batch pages, third-party assay results published whether or not they're flattering, a named quality lead who exists and can be contacted, an adverse-event line that is staffed by a human and whose number appears on the pack rather than on page four of the website.

These are claims about our own process, which are the only claims in this category that are both unrestricted and verifiable. And they describe an asset a competitor needs years to build, not a message they need a quarter to copy.

**5. The cancellation promise — a bet against the category's own business model.**
The most predatory mechanic in Japanese supplement marketing is the subscription trap: a first month at a token price, a minimum commitment buried in the terms, cancellation by telephone only, during business hours, into a queue. It generates a large share of the category's consumer complaints and a large share of its revenue, and those are the same customers.

I'd make the opposite the headline. One tap. No call. No minimum. Cancel from the confirmation email if you like. And say it in the advertisement, at the same size as the product name.

This is an ethics policy disguised as a marketing idea, or the reverse, and I'd rather not settle which. What matters is that it deletes a revenue line that our own forecast probably contains. That fight is worth having in month one, in daylight, rather than in month fourteen when someone quietly reintroduces a retention friction to hit a number.

**6. The parent problem — a bet on a relationship, handled carefully.**
